## Policies

### Peer Review

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Type** | Double-anonymous: authors and reviewers both stay anonymous; every submission is by default reviewed by at least 2 external reviewers (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/review-process, retrieved 2026-11-23). Reviewers may choose to sign; co-reviewing by a junior colleague is allowed with editor approval (same page) |
| **Transferable / Cascade?** | Blank. No source read |
| **Reviewer reports published?** | Blank. The review-process page read says nothing about publishing reports (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/review-process, retrieved 2026-11-23) |
| **Typical R+R rounds** | SciRev, n = 5: an average of 1.6 review rounds (https://scirev.org/journal/language/, retrieved 2026-11-23). The Editors' Report tracks separate decision times for minor and major revision requests, so revision rounds are a normal outcome (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123) |
| **Reviewer recommendations** | The reviewers' guidance asks for a clear recommendation to the editor: accept, minor revisions, major revisions or reject (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/instructions-for-peer-reviewers, retrieved 2026-11-23). The same page asks reviewers to consider topic appropriateness for a generalist journal, theoretical contribution, embedding in previous research, and methodology. An appeal route exists: to appeal, contact the editors; it is reviewed by at least one editor who did not review the manuscript originally (review-process page above) |

### AI Policy

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Has journal-specific AI policy?** | Partly. The journal's preparing-your-materials page has its own section, "Use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools", written under the Cambridge University Press research publishing ethics guidelines (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials, retrieved 2026-11-23) |
| **Explicit permission gate?** | No gate found. Use is allowed with declaration |
| **Leniency (1-5)** | 3 (allowed with mandatory declaration for generative uses; same rubric as the Mind entry) |
| **Summary** | AI tools cannot be listed as authors. Authors must declare and describe any use of an AI tool to generate text or images (including translation) or to analyse or extract insights from data; minimal non-generative uses such as spelling or language checking need no declaration. The declaration goes in the acknowledgements or a footnote (text), the methods (data analysis) or figure captions (images), and names the tool and version, dates, how it can be accessed, and a full description of use. For reviewers: manuscripts and reviews must not be shared with any AI tool and AI help is limited to minimal non-generative uses. Retrieved 2026-11-23 |
| **Source URL** | https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials ; reviewers: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/instructions-for-peer-reviewers |

## Format

> Source for the rules below: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials and https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/submitting-your-materials, read with curl on 2026-11-23.

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Article types accepted** | General Research Article, Research Report, Language and Public Policy, Language Revitalization and Documentation, Teaching Linguistics, Perspectives (target article plus commentaries and rejoinder), Commentary, Rejoinder; by invitation only: Presidential Address, Book Review, Review Article (preparing-your-materials page). The submission count by section for 2025 was 158 general research articles, 17 research reports, 10 teaching linguistics, 9 commentary, replies and letters, 8 revitalization and documentation, 8 perspectives, 5 language and public policy (total 215) (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123) |
| **Word limit** | General Research Article: must not exceed 18,000 words including notes, tables and appendices but excluding references; over 12,000 words is assessed by the editor for appropriateness of length and may get a more stringent review. Research Report under 9,000 words (same inclusions). Teaching Linguistics 10,000 words (excluding references, appendices and supplements). Perspectives 10,000 words and Commentary or Rejoinder 5,000, both including references and appendices. Review Article 5,000 words excluding references; Book Review 2,000 to 4,000. The summary table in the same page says "ideally max. 12,000, but up to 18,000 words under special circumstance" for general research articles |
| **Word limit negotiability** | The page says the 12,000-18,000 word range is allowed "under special circumstance" and that long manuscripts may be returned for revision before review; authors with previously published components are told to contact the editor beforehand. No wider statement on exceptions |
| **Abstract limit** | Maximum 200 words; 5 to 7 keywords; book reviews and rejoinders carry neither; a cover letter is required that briefly makes the case for relevance to Language |
| **Reference limit** | No cap; the page asks authors to keep references within a reasonable limit and to include only directly relevant sources. Style is the LSA Journals Referencing Style (author-year, full first names in the reference list). Initial submissions need not follow the style sheet; accepted manuscripts must conform |
| **Supplementary material** | Supplementary materials are published online with the article, are not typeset or copyedited and cannot be changed except by correction; Teaching Linguistics submissions are expected to include them |
| **Figure/Table limits** | No count limit found. Figures and tables are embedded in the single main-document PDF at submission; titles and notes must be self-explanatory and sourced; accessibility standard WCAG 2.1 AA applies to published material |
| **Style / submission format** | Submission through ScholarOne only (https://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/lsa-language). Initial anonymised manuscript as a single PDF, double-spaced if not LaTeX-generated; cover letter also PDF. On acceptance: de-anonymised PDF plus Word or LaTeX source (LaTeX style files are provided). American English spelling, single quotation marks, serial comma, sentence-case titles, Leipzig glossing rules for glossed examples, LSA inclusive-language guidelines (authors may be asked to revise nonconforming manuscripts before review). ORCID is required for the corresponding author |

### Framing Requirements

- **Mandatory framing?** One scope condition is stated by the journal itself: Language is a general journal for the Society's membership, manuscripts "should be made as readable as possible to non-specialists", and papers that appear addressed to and understandable by only those in narrow specialties will likely be returned unreviewed with a recommendation to submit to a more specialized journal (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials, retrieved 2026-11-23). The reviewers' guidance asks whether the manuscript has broad, general appeal and makes a meaningful contribution to the development of linguistic theory (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/instructions-for-peer-reviewers).
- **What kind of engagement?** For a General Research Article, a contribution to the development of linguistic theory, broadly defined, written so that a non-specialist grasps the gist and why it matters to linguistics; the Research Report section is for data-driven or methodological-innovation pieces that still engage the theoretical literature and are not "work in progress" (preparing-your-materials page above). The journal also points to the editorial "What Makes a Paper Appropriate for Language?" by Coetzee and Beavers, Language 97(2), 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1353/lan.2021.0016). The DOI resolves to a Cambridge page whose 4-page PDF downloaded with plain curl (browser User-Agent, cookie jar, referer set to the article page) and was read in full on 2026-11-23. It says: a paper that could be imagined at the LSA annual meeting is most likely a good thematic fit, and all subdisciplines and theoretical approaches are welcome; the journal names neurolinguistics, anthropological linguistics, raciolinguistics and language and gender among underrepresented areas and invites submissions there; a paper must contribute to linguistic theory, with "theory" taken very broadly, so a primarily descriptive paper may not fit, while the Research Reports section takes data or method papers that develop theory less; the framing must address a generalist audience even if the middle of the paper stays technical; and the length limit for regular research papers was then a strict 18,000 words excluding references and supplementary material, with about 12,000 encouraged and manuscripts over 16,000 under additional scrutiny. That 2021 length wording differs from the current instructions summarised in Format, which should be preferred.
- **Article type and length**: see Format. Two-paper cap: at most two papers in review at once, at least one of them co-authored; no simultaneous submission elsewhere (preparing-your-materials page above).
- **Section framing seen**: Language and Public Policy asks for scholarship on public-policy areas that involve language as topic, focus, instrument or variable; Teaching Linguistics asks authors to state their positionality and institutional context and how applicable the approach is outside it (same page).
- **Consequences of ignoring it**: stated by the journal for the scope condition only: unreviewed return with a recommendation to go to a specialized journal (preparing-your-materials page above). The share of returns is not published; SciRev has no immediate-rejection time for this journal (https://scirev.org/journal/language/).

### Methodological Preferences

> Counts: regex matches over title plus abstract of Crossref records of this journal dated 2021-11-23 to 2026-11-23 (published-date filter, see Orientation); 164 of 240 records have an abstract, so counts are lower bounds; shares use 164 as the denominator. Scoring convention of this research pass (its own, not an external standard): share 0 = 0; under 1% = 1; 1-5% = 2; over 5% = 3; 4-5 only with a cited editorial statement. Scores measure how often a method appears in the abstracts, not how a reviewer would judge it. The schema's rows come from the social sciences; where a row does not fit linguistics it says so, and rows for linguistic method families are added. Regexes are R1 to R26 in AI-Research Notes.

| Method | Receptiveness (0-5) | Evidence |
|--------|---------------------|----------|
| Quantitative experimental | 3 | "experiment, experimental" 24 (14.6%, R1); statistical terms (regression, mixed-effects, Bayesian, statistical) 13 (7.9%, R4). The instructions say empirical or experimental studies should allow replication from the article, references and possibly supplementary materials (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials) |
| Qualitative interviews | 2 | "interview, ethnograph-, participant observation" 4 (2.4%, R7) of 164. The row fits only partly: interview work is mostly in the sociolinguistic and revitalization strands |
| Autoethnography | 0 | 0 of 164 (R23). The row does not fit this journal's content; no editorial statement |
| Theoretical / Conceptual | 4 | Score 4 rests on an editorial statement, not a count: general research articles are expected to contribute to linguistic theory broadly defined (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials; reviewer criterion at https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/instructions-for-peer-reviewers). Counts: "theoretical" 13 (7.9%, R18), "formal, formalism, formalization" 10 (6.1%, R19), "we or I propose, argue, show, claim, demonstrate" 52 (31.7%, R17) |
| Mixed methods | 0 | 0 of 164 (R25). The row does not fit; no statement either way |
| Meta-analysis | 1 | "meta-analysis, systematic review" 1 (0.6%, R21b). The row does not fit linguistics well; a Review Article section exists but is by invitation only |
| Formal linguistic analysis (judgment-based, added row) | 3 | Sub-field mentions: syntax 31 (18.9%, R9), semantics or pragmatics 21 (12.8%, R11), phonology or phonetics 34 (20.7%, R10). "acceptability or grammaticality judgment" appears in only 3 (1.8%, R2), because judgment data are usually not named in abstracts; the instructions tell authors reporting judgments to be ready to substantiate them (preparing-your-materials page above) |
| Corpus / computational modelling (added row) | 3 | "corpus, corpora" 16 (9.8%, R3); computational, simulation, neural or language-model wording 7 (4.3%, R5). The 2025 Editors' Report shows author-selected computational linguistics at 7, 5 and 1 submissions in 2023, 2024 and 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123) |
| Fieldwork / documentation (added row) | 2 | "fieldwork, language documentation, documentary, elicitation" 5 (3.0%, R6); a dedicated section exists and the instructions list the metadata required for original field work: where, when, how collected, and speaker characteristics (preparing-your-materials page above) |

### Voice & Style

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **First-person voice acceptance (0-5)** | Not scored. Sample (abstract-only text; titles and full texts not searched): 21 of the 30 most recent Crossref records with an abstract (published 2025-09-01 to 2026-10-26) contain I, we, our or my (regex R26, case-sensitive); across all 164 abstracts in the window 127 do (Crossref works API, window 2021-11-23 to 2026-11-23, retrieved 2026-11-23). Examples with first person: https://doi.org/10.1017/s0097850726000159 ("In this article, I argue"), https://doi.org/10.1017/s009785072600007x (We present a case study), https://doi.org/10.1017/s0097850726000081 ("In this article, I describe"). The anonymisation advice runs the other way for the submitted manuscript: authors should avoid referring to themselves in the first person and may change such passages back after acceptance (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/review-process) |
| **Expected density** | Length ceilings are in Format: up to 18,000 words for general research articles (ideally 12,000), 9,000 for research reports, excluding references for those two types. Readability for non-specialists is an explicit requirement (preparing-your-materials page, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials) |
| **Abstract and keywords** | Maximum 200 words; 5 to 7 keywords; cover letter required (same page) |
| **Writing style notes** | Same page: American spelling; single quotation marks; serial comma; sentence-case titles with the subtitle run in after a colon; abbreviations spelled out at first use; "e.g.", "i.e." only inside parentheses; transcriptions in square brackets or slashes; non-Latin scripts transliterated; non-English examples glossed word by word with a free translation in single quotes, following the Leipzig Glossing Rules; numbered examples on separate lines; references in the LSA author-year style with full given names |
| **Authorship pattern** | Crossref author-field counts for the 240 records in the window (book reviews and front matter included): 1 author 92, 2 authors 43, 3 authors 35, 4 or more 25, no author listed 45 (retrieved 2026-11-23) |

### Reviewer Pool Characteristics

Reviewer behaviour itself is not observable from public pages; what follows is what public pages do show.

| Aspect | Detail | Evidence |
|--------|--------|----------|
| **Dominant tradition** | Board of 24 entries across general linguistics sub-fields and four sections (counts above); the 2025 Editors' Report thanks associate editors who handle general research articles and research reports and separate associate editors for special sections (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123). The board lists no discipline labels, so a discipline count is not possible | https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/about-this-journal/editorial-board |
| **Reviewer list size** | The Editors' Report for 2025 names 135 individuals who refereed submissions in 2025, 6 of them marked as having provided more than one review; countries and affiliations are not listed (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123, names counted from the page on 2026-11-23) | https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123 |
| **Review model** | Double-anonymous, at least 2 external reviewers (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/review-process). The reviewers' page adds that in a field as small as linguistics reviewers may guess authors and are asked not to assume identity or inspect metadata | https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/instructions-for-peer-reviewers |
| **Reviewer competence variance** | Blank as a judgement. Self-reported SciRev figures, n = 5: difficulty of reviewer comments 4.5 of 5, quality of review reports 3.8 of 5, 2.8 reports on average (https://scirev.org/journal/language/, retrieved 2026-11-23). The five entries differ widely (3 reports and 5 reports per manuscript; one acceptance with no reports sent); n is too small to describe variance | https://scirev.org/journal/language/ ; https://scirev.org/reviews/language/ |
| **Quantitative mindset bias on qualitative work?** | Blank. No source on reviewer attitudes; the abstract counts show interview-based work is rare (R7), which cannot tell how reviewers treat it | Crossref counts, see Methodological Preferences |
| **Discourse community signals (author side)** | Author community as a proxy, not a reviewer list: United States 33, Germany 12, United Kingdom 9 of the 239 articles in the window (OpenAlex, not independently re-run). On the live board, 18 of 24 entries are in the USA | OpenAlex works API, retrieved 2026-11-23; board page https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/about-this-journal/editorial-board |

### Sensitive Topics

> Counts are regex matches (R-labels in AI-Research Notes) over title plus abstract of 164 Crossref records with an abstract, published 2021-11-23 to 2026-11-23; lower bounds. "Receptiveness" gives frequency; High is used only where the journal states a position or runs a dedicated section.

| Topic Category | Receptiveness | Evidence |
|----------------|---------------|----------|
| Indigenous languages, documentation and revitalization | High | Dedicated section "Language Revitalization and Documentation" and an instruction on research involving Native American or other Indigenous peoples (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials); 11 of 164 abstract-records (6.7%, R15); 8 submissions to the section in 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0097850726000123) |
| Language and public policy | High | Dedicated section (same instructions page); "language policy, public policy" 5 (3.0%, R15b); 5 submissions in 2025 |
| Gender | Present | 11 (6.7%, R16a; includes grammatical gender); the instructions require the LSA guidelines on inclusive language and on avoiding misgendering |
| Race and raciolinguistics | Rare in abstracts | 1 (0.6%, R16b); one 2026 article on race and ethnicity information in research (https://doi.org/10.1017/s0097850726000093); the 2025 Editors' Report lists raciolinguistics as an author-selected area with 0 submissions in 2024 and 2025 and 1 in 2023 |
| Sexual and gender minorities | Rare | 0 (0.0%, R16c) of 164 |
| AI and large language models | Rare in this window | 0 (0.0%, R20b) of 164 abstract-records; computational or modelling wording 7 (4.3%, R5); no call on AI found |
| Sign languages | Present | "sign language" 16 (9.8%, R13); sign linguistics 4, 2 and 5 submissions in 2023, 2024 and 2025 (Editors' Report) |
| Teaching linguistics (including justice, equity, diversity and inclusion) | High | Dedicated section whose evaluation criteria ask how justice, equity, diversity and inclusion issues are addressed where relevant (preparing-your-materials page above); 10 submissions in 2025 (Editors' Report) |

### Practical Concerns

| Concern | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| **IRB requirement strictness** | Every accepted paper needs a short ethics statement (50 to 80 words); research with human participants, tissue or data should be approved by the relevant institutional ethics committee, and the committee name, approval number and consent types go in the statement; where approval was waived, the waiving committee is named; otherwise the statement reads "Ethical approval was not required" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials, retrieved 2026-11-23) |
| **Single-author acceptance** | Single-author papers are common: 92 of the 240 Crossref records in the window (45 list no author; book reviews and front matter are included). Cap rule: an author may not have two sole-authored manuscripts in review at once, and at most two papers in review of which at least one is co-authored (preparing-your-materials page above) |
| **Independent scholar friendliness** | Affiliation rule: affiliations should be the institution(s) where the research was conducted, supported or approved, and for non-research content the current affiliation (preparing-your-materials page above); no independent-scholar rule is stated. APC waivers and discounts are decided by Cambridge, separately from the editorial decision (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/journal-policies/open-access-options) |
| **Data transparency requirement** | A Data Availability Statement is mandatory for every manuscript, placed before the references; sharing in a repository is encouraged and code sharing strongly encouraged; if data cannot be shared the statement must say why (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/journal-policies/research-transparency, retrieved 2026-11-23). Field notes, replicable empirical studies and reported judgments carry extra expectations (preparing-your-materials page above) |
| **OPSEC compatibility** | Double-anonymous: the manuscript and cover letter are submitted as PDF only (no LaTeX source or word-processor file), file metadata should be cleaned, and no acknowledgements should be added while under review; the editors do not check all files for anonymity and return documents that are visibly not anonymised (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/peer-review-information/review-process, retrieved 2026-11-23). Preprints are allowed anywhere at any time (open-access-options page above) |
| **AI use** | Declaration required for generative uses; AI cannot be an author (see AI Policy; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials) |
| **Open access and cost** | Gold OA only since 2026: APC GBP 2610 or USD 3655, 15% less for LSA members, with institutional-agreement, equity, Research4Life and waiver routes (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/fees-and-pricing) |
| **Prior publication** | Papers published elsewhere or under review elsewhere are not considered, including translations; results previously in working papers or proceedings may be considered if the paper develops them along new lines or in greater depth, and the editor should be contacted first (preparing-your-materials page above) |

**Method notes:** keyword counts were recomputed on 2026-11-23 from Crossref: 240 journal-article records with publication date 2021-11-23 to 2026-11-23, of which 164 carry an abstract; abstract markup was stripped, the title and abstract were searched with the regexes below (Python re, flag IGNORECASE except R26, which searches the abstract only and is case-sensitive); share = hits / 164. The earlier OpenAlex tallies (279 records, 183 with abstract, rebuilt from abstract_inverted_index) did not reproduce and were replaced; remaining OpenAlex figures are marked not independently re-run. Regex hits count records, not occurrences. Broad patterns over-count: R16a matches grammatical gender, R14 matches "child", R24 matches "students".

- R5 `\b(computational|simulation|neural|machine learning|language models?)\b` ; R6 `\b(fieldwork|field work|language documentation|documentary|elicitation)\b` ; R7 `\b(interviews?|ethnograph\w*|participant observation)\b`
- R9 `\b(syntax|syntactic)\b` ; R10 `\b(phonolog\w*|phonetic\w*|prosod\w*)\b` ; R11 `\b(semantic\w*|pragmatic\w*)\b` ; R12 `\bsociolinguistic\w*\b` (9 records, 5.5% of 164)

- R20 `\b(eye[- ]track\w*|ERP|EEG|fMRI|neuro\w*)\b` ; R20b `\b(artificial intelligence|large language models?|LLMs?|ChatGPT|GPT-?\d?)\b` ; R21 `\b(universal grammar|generative|minimalist)\b` ; R21b `\b(meta-analys[ei]s|systematic review)\b`

## Strategic Notes

> Each statement below follows from a fact recorded above and names it. Where the evidence does not support a statement, the field says so.

### Hard Blockers

- **Audience scope**: the journal states that manuscripts addressed only to narrow specialties will likely be returned unreviewed (Framing Requirements; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/language/information/author-instructions/preparing-your-materials).
- **Length**: general research articles must not exceed 18,000 words excluding references, research reports 9,000 (Format).
- **Prior and parallel publication**: work published or under review elsewhere is not considered and a violation is rejected whatever the stage (Practical Concerns, Prior publication).
- **Mandatory statements**: ethics statement (50 to 80 words) and Data Availability Statement for every manuscript (Practical Concerns).
- **Anonymisation**: documents that are visibly not anonymised are returned before any editorial action (Practical Concerns, OPSEC compatibility).
- **AI use**: undeclared generative AI use breaches the policy (AI Policy).

### Soft Tax

- **Time**: SciRev reports first review rounds of 21.1 to 43.3 weeks (n = 5) and the journal's own 2025 figures show 242 days on average for major-revision decisions (Review Cycle Time). The two measures are not the same and not reconciled, but both point to months, not weeks.
- **Cost**: all articles are gold open access since 2026 with an APC of GBP 2610 or USD 3655 unless covered by an agreement, funding or waiver, which Cambridge decides separately from the editors (Open Access).
- **Rewriting**: authors must prepare an anonymised PDF first and a de-anonymised, LSA-style-conforming version on acceptance, with full first names in references (Format, Voice & Style).
- **Submission cap**: at most two papers in review, one of them co-authored (Framing Requirements).

### Best Suited For

- Theoretically motivated general-linguistics research articles that can be made understandable to non-specialists: required by the instructions (Framing Requirements, Methodological Preferences) and consistent with the mix of syntax, phonology, semantics, experimental and corpus work in the abstracts (Orientation).
- Documentation, revitalization, language-policy and linguistics-teaching scholarship, which have dedicated sections with stated criteria (Format, Sensitive Topics).
- Authors who can cover or have waived an APC (Open Access).

### Not Recommended For

- Work meant for a single sub-community and unable to speak to general linguistics: the instructions say such papers are returned (Framing Requirements).
- Authors who need a predictable turnaround: the available figures run to many months (Review Cycle Time); no acceptance rate is published, so odds cannot be stated.
- Interview-based qualitative, mixed-methods or autoethnographic studies as a primary route: interview wording appears in 4 of 164 abstract-records and mixed methods and autoethnography in 0 (Methodological Preferences); this shows rarity, not rejection.

### Rejection Fallback Chain

> No source states where rejected authors usually go. The rows below are topical neighbours that already exist in this corpus, listed only because they share subject area; they are not a claim about acceptance odds. The journal itself tells authors of narrow-specialty papers to use a more specialized journal (Framing Requirements).

| Rank | Journal | Why this fallback works |
|------|---------|------------------------|
| 1 | [Linguistics and Philosophy](linguistics-and-philosophy.md) | Same field (theoretical linguistics, semantics); an entry exists in this corpus. No fit evidence collected here |
| 2 | [Journal of Child Language](../psychology/journal-of-child-language.md) | Topical neighbour for acquisition work; an entry exists in this corpus. No fit evidence collected here |
| 3 | [Computational Linguistics](../cognitive-science/computational-linguistics.md) | Topical neighbour for computational and corpus work; an entry exists in this corpus. No fit evidence collected here |
